# Routing model traffic with Jev and agentgateway

Put a classifier in front of model selection so the gateway picks the model each request deserves. Rewrite the model in the request body from an ExtProc server, watch three different failures behave three different ways, then build a cache, measure what it got wrong, and take it out again.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=jev-model-routing&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-model-routing_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

Eligible paid Zenable customers get an OpenRouter key automatically in their sandbox. Take the hosted version of this lab, with the key already configured, at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=jev-model-routing&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-model-routing_readme.

**Duration** 72 minutes · **Difficulty** Advanced

**Topics** `Agent Protocols` · `Guardrails & Policy` · `How LLMs Work`

**Prerequisites**

- The Judging code with typed questions in Jev lab, or equivalent familiarity with Noul, Choice and Score
- The Seeing and Governing MCP traffic with agentgateway lab, or comfort with agentgateway's config vocabulary
- Docker, git, and comfort reading YAML and Python
- A TypeSafe or OpenRouter key, or the recorded decisions this rig ships
- For the last section only, an OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini key, or the recorded alignment run this rig ships

## Set up AI inference

Your sandbox has no hosted AI key. Automatic keys require an eligible paid plan and an available inference budget. Choose your own OpenRouter key, or use the local model and the lab's recorded-answer steps.

### Option A: use your own OpenRouter key

Create a key at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys). Then run this in the sandbox terminal, with your key in place of `sk-or-...`:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference sk-or-...
```

The command writes your key and the model settings into `~/.env` and configures every coding agent installed on the sandbox. Open a new terminal so your shell picks them up.

> [!WARNING]
> Your key goes in `~/.env`, never in the lab directory. Every attendee in the sandbox network can read the lab remote, and a key committed there is a key you've shared.

### Option B: use local Ollama (no key)

The sandbox runs [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) with a small model, `qwen3-nothink`, already downloaded and built. Point every agent at it:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference --ollama
```

Then open a new terminal. The model runs on the sandbox's CPU, so expect slower and weaker answers than a hosted model gives you. This option configures coding agents only. For steps that call Jev directly, follow the lab's recorded-answer instructions, such as adding `--fixtures` where shown. Those commands do not switch to recordings automatically.

For Option B, install Ollama from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download). `qwen3:1.7b` is a reasoning model, and thinking makes it very slow on a CPU, so the steps below build a copy with thinking turned off.

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

Then set the variables below in your environment, for example in a `~/.env` file that your shell loads with `set -a; . ~/.env; set +a`. Claude Code reads the `ANTHROPIC_*` variables, and agents that speak the OpenAI API, such as Codex, read `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

## Getting started

_~8 min · Hands-on_

Let's get the rig and its two models:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
  || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
uv sync --locked --project router
```

Both models run on your own machine through Ollama, and the gateway calls them from inside a container. Ollama answers on loopback only, which nothing in a container can reach, so point it at every interface first:

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d
printf '[Service]\nEnvironment="OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434"\n' \
  | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/listen.conf > /dev/null
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ollama
timeout 90 bash -c 'until curl -fsS http://localhost:11434/api/version >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done'
```

That edits a service on your machine, and the Cleanup section puts it back.

Now the two models, one obviously cheaper than the other. Run these on their own and let each finish, because the progress display swallows anything pasted behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:0.6b
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Now the credential. The router reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` from the shell that starts its container, and every new terminal exports them from `~/.env`. On a Zenable sandbox the hosted key is already there; anywhere else, the setup section at the top of this lab covers it. If the key arrived after you opened this terminal, open a new one and come back to this directory.

To run without a key, select the recorded decisions in `router.env`. This file holds the router's settings, and it's where we turn knobs later:

```bash
echo 'JEV_FIXTURES=1' > router.env
```

Now bring the stack up on a config with two models and nothing choosing between them:

```bash
cp 01-baseline.yaml config.yaml
docker compose up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
```

```console
NAME           IMAGE                      COMMAND                  SERVICE        CREATED         STATUS                   PORTS
agentgateway   jev-routing-agentgateway   "/app/agentgateway -…"   agentgateway   5 seconds ago   Up 2 seconds (healthy)   127.0.0.1:4000->4000/tcp
jev-router     jev-routing-jev-router     "uv run --no-sync py…"   jev-router     5 seconds ago   Up 4 seconds (healthy)   9090/tcp
```

Two containers, and only the gateway publishes a port. The router is reachable on the compose network and nowhere else, which suits something upstream calls part of its trust boundary.

> [!TIP]
> agentgateway's admin API on 15000 binds to loopback inside its container, so publishing that port gets you an empty reply. `docker compose exec agentgateway /usr/bin/busybox wget -qO - http://127.0.0.1:15000/api/config` reads it from the inside.

Two requests we'll send several times over, so let's put them in files:

```bash
cat > mechanical.json <<'EOF'
{"model":"auto","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Rename the variable `cfg` to `config` in src/app.py and update the two call sites."}]}
EOF
cat > deliberative.json <<'EOF'
{"model":"auto","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Our checkout service times out under load about once an hour and the logs show no errors. How should we work out what is going wrong?"}]}
EOF
```

Neither one names a model. Send them both:

```bash
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @mechanical.json | jq -r .model
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
```

```console
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @mechanical.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:0.6b
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:0.6b
```

Both land on the small model, because `auto` resolves to `qwen-small` and nothing looked at what either request asked for. Diagnosing an hourly timeout on a 0.6B model is what we're here to fix.

## Putting a classifier in front of model selection

_~12 min · Hands-on_

The router asks one Choice with one option per model, and the option names are the model names, so the answer is already the string that goes into the request body. The criteria text separates them:

```json
{
  "question": "Which model should answer `request.newest_message`? Judge only the newest message; `request.prior_turns` is context for what it refers to, never the thing being routed.",
  "focus": "Decide on the reasoning the answer needs, not on the topic, the tone, or the length of `request.newest_message`. A request that names the exact edit to make needs no deliberation even when the edit is large. A request that states a goal and leaves the approach open needs deliberation even when it is one sentence.",
  "models": [
    {
      "name": "qwen-small",
      "criterion": "The newest user message asks for a mechanical transformation that a competent engineer would finish without stopping to think: renaming or reformatting code, converting between two named formats, extracting values that are already written down in the message, translating prose, or answering a single factual question whose answer the message already contains. Length alone does not qualify a request for this option; a long but mechanical request still belongs here."
    },
    {
      "name": "qwen-large",
      "criterion": "The newest user message cannot be answered until something is worked out first: weighing a trade-off between two approaches, designing something that does not exist yet, diagnosing a fault from evidence that does not name the cause, reasoning about consequences the message does not state, or producing code whose correctness depends on a rule that has to be derived. Shortness does not disqualify a request from this option; a one-line question can still need deliberation."
    }
  ]
}
```

That file is the policy. `catalog.py` loads it, hashes it into the fingerprint, and sends it as the `criteria` block of one Choice question, so an edit to a criterion is a diff a reviewer reads rather than a change buried in a program.

<details>
<summary>The whole catalogue, question and fingerprint, from `router/jev_router/catalog.py`</summary>

```python
"""Copyright (c) 2026 Zenable, Inc. The model catalogue, and the routing question written over it.

The criteria text IS the routing policy. Jev answers the question as written,
literally, so widening one option's description is a policy change, and it
lives in `policy.json` beside this module where a diff of a proposed edit is a
diff of the policy rather than a diff of the program that sends it.

`jev_router.align` writes that file from an accepted jev-align run, so an
aligned definition reaches the router the same way a hand edit does.
"""

import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

POLICY_FILE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "policy.json"


class CandidateModel(BaseModel):
    """One model agentgateway can route to, and the case for choosing it."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True, strict=True)

    name: str
    """The name in `llm.models[].name`. Jev returns this string verbatim."""

    criterion: str
    """What kind of request belongs on this model. Read literally by Jev."""


class RoutingPolicy(BaseModel):
    """Everything about the question this router asks, as one reviewable object."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True, strict=True)

    question: str

    focus: str = ""
    """A second field Jev reads as part of the same instructions. An aligned
    policy usually arrives as one block of instructions and leaves this empty,
    which is a different question from the one with it and fingerprints as one."""

    models: tuple[CandidateModel, ...]
    """Ordered cheapest first. The order is not a tie-break: Jev returns a full
    distribution and the caller takes the argmax. It decides the fallback."""


def load_policy(path: Path = POLICY_FILE) -> RoutingPolicy:
    return RoutingPolicy.model_validate_json(path.read_text())


POLICY: RoutingPolicy = load_policy()

CATALOG: tuple[CandidateModel, ...] = POLICY.models

MODEL_NAMES: frozenset[str] = frozenset(model.name for model in CATALOG)

QUESTION_ID = "route"

QUESTION_TEXT = POLICY.question

QUESTION_FOCUS = POLICY.focus


def build_questions() -> dict[str, object]:
    """The `questions` block of a `/v1/systemone` request."""
    instructions: dict[str, str] = {"question": QUESTION_TEXT}
    if QUESTION_FOCUS:
        instructions["focus"] = QUESTION_FOCUS
    return {
        QUESTION_ID: {
            "type": "choice",
            "instructions": instructions,
            "criteria": {model.name: model.criterion for model in CATALOG},
        }
    }


def policy_fingerprint(jev_model: str) -> str:
    """Identity of everything that can change a routing answer but the request.

    Every cache entry is keyed under this, so editing a criterion, the question,
    the candidate set, or the Jev model id invalidates the whole cache at once.
    A TTL cannot do that: the stale entries would outlive the policy that
    produced them for as long as the TTL runs.
    """
    payload = json.dumps(
        {"jev_model": jev_model, "questions": build_questions()},
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
    )
    return hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
```

Both criteria spend their last sentence on the boundary case, because Jev reads them literally and length is the first thing it reaches for as a stand-in for difficulty when nothing rules that out.

</details>

Attaching the router to the gateway is nine lines, which `02-routed.yaml` adds to the config you already have:

```yaml
llm:
  policies:
    extProc:
      host: jev-router:9090
      failureMode: failOpen
      processingOptions:
        requestHeaderMode: send
        responseHeaderMode: skip
        requestBodyMode: buffered
        responseBodyMode: none
        requestTrailerMode: skip
        responseTrailerMode: skip
```

`requestBodyMode: buffered` matters, because the default delivers the body in pieces and the router needs all of it before there's JSON to parse. Everything on the response side is off, since a routing decision has nothing to say about the reply.

```bash
cp 02-routed.yaml config.yaml
docker compose restart agentgateway
docker compose up -d --wait agentgateway
```

> [!WARNING]
> Attaching an ExtProc policy needs that restart. Copy the file over and the admin API will show the new policy within a second, while the data plane carries on with the old one and every request skips the router without a word in any log.

Now the same two requests, plus the second one again:

```bash
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @mechanical.json | jq -r .model
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
```

```console
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @mechanical.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:0.6b
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:1.7b
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:1.7b
```

Success! 🎉 Two requests that differ only in what they asked for, and two different models answering. Neither request named a model, and neither did the client that sent it.

Here's what decided it:

```bash
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'route ->' | tail -3
```

```console
15:03:12 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-small  src=jev      conf=0.99 {'qwen-small': 0.99, 'qwen-large': 0.01}
15:03:13 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-large  src=jev      conf=1.00 {'qwen-small': 0.0, 'qwen-large': 1.0}
15:03:13 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-large  src=exact    conf=1.00 {'qwen-small': 0.0, 'qwen-large': 1.0}
```

Three decisions, and only two of them asked Jev. The third says `src=exact`, the router's cache answering a request it had already seen. We come back to that in the last section.

The gateway agrees about where the requests went, which is the part an operator sees:

```bash
docker compose logs agentgateway --no-log-prefix | grep -o 'gen_ai.request.model=[^ ]*' | tail -3
```

```console
gen_ai.request.model=qwen3:0.6b
gen_ai.request.model=qwen3:1.7b
gen_ai.request.model=qwen3:1.7b
```

The router also sets an `x-jev-route` header carrying the model, the source and the confidence, so the decision travels with the request into whatever reads your traces.

Question: the rewrite happens in the request body, and the gateway's own model router reads that same body afterwards. What has to be true about the two of them for this to work at all, and what would you expect to see if it weren't?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The processor has to run before model selection, and the model router has to read the body the processor wrote rather than the one the client sent. agentgateway's schema commits to the first, and this section is the second happening.

When the second one breaks, nothing complains. The router logs a sensible decision, the gateway ignores it, and every request goes to whatever the client's `model` already resolved to.

That's what an upstream bug fixed after the current stable release did, which is why `Dockerfile.gateway` pins an alpha rather than the tag you'd reach for by habit.

</details>

## Three ways this can let you down

_~12 min · Hands-on_

A judgment on the request path is a network call on the request path. Let's break it three different ways, because they need three different answers.

First, point the router at a port with nothing behind it:

```bash
echo 'JEV_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:9099' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -2
```

```console
$ echo 'JEV_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:9099' >> router.env
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
 Container jev-router Recreate
 Container jev-router Recreated
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
 Container jev-router Waiting
 Container jev-router Healthy
$ curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
http=200  total=0.085234s
$ docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -2
15:03:15 WARNING jev_router.decide jev call failed, routing to qwen-small: All connection attempts failed
15:03:15 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-small  src=fallback conf=0.00
```

The request completed on the cheap model, with one line at WARNING and nothing at ERROR. The refused connection cost almost nothing: the total is about what the small model takes to answer on its own, which is well under a second here and around a second on a sandbox's CPU.

The caller carries on down the path it would have taken anyway, and the log says once that a decision was skipped. Our deliberative question went to the small model, which is the cost of the outage.

Now take away the router itself, so the gateway's own fail-open has to handle it:

```bash
docker compose stop jev-router
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
docker compose start jev-router
```

```console
$ docker compose stop jev-router
 Container jev-router Stopping
 Container jev-router Stopped
$ curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
http=200  total=10.107756s
$ docker compose start jev-router
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
```

Also a 200, and this one took ten seconds. `failureMode` decides whether the request survives and says nothing about what it costs. Every second of that was the gateway resolving a name that no longer exists, and `failClosed` would have spent the same ten seconds before its 500.

Notice what the request carried while that was happening. The body still said `"model": "auto"` when it reached the model router, which is the whole job of the `auto` virtual model in both configs.

It looks redundant while the router works, because nothing ever reaches it.

The third failure is the one worth the rest of this section. Start a stand-in for Jev that accepts the connection, reads the request, and then never answers:

```bash
nohup uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.standin --mode hang > standin.log 2>&1 &
sleep 2
echo 'JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS=600' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
```

We've also raised the router's own deadline out of the way, so nothing in this stack is bounding the call. Send one request:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' --max-time 60 http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
```

```console
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 60007 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
http=000  total=60.007577s
```

Sixty seconds, no bytes, and the client gave up first. `failOpen` never fired, because nothing failed: the processor is connected, healthy, and still thinking.

Upstream has this open as [issue #3412](https://github.com/agentgateway/agentgateway/issues/3412), and the maintainers are clear that Envoy's per-message timeout is ignored, so there is nothing in the gateway's config that would have saved this request.

What saves it lives in the processor. Put the deadline back:

```bash
sed -i '/JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS/d' router.env
echo 'JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS=1.5' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -2
```

```console
$ sed -i '/JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS/d' router.env
$ echo 'JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS=1.5' >> router.env
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
 Container jev-router Recreate
 Container jev-router Recreated
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
 Container jev-router Waiting
 Container jev-router Healthy
$ curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
http=200  total=1.607945s
$ docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -2
15:04:36 WARNING jev_router.decide jev call failed, routing to qwen-small: TimeoutError
15:04:36 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-small  src=fallback conf=0.00
```

Same silent stand-in, same request, and now it completes on the fallback model with a `TimeoutError` in the log. The deadline turned an unbounded wait into a bounded one, and it did that from inside the processor because that's the only place with a say.

Question: the first failure added next to nothing to the request and the second added ten seconds.

Both answered 200, both were `failOpen`, and nothing about the gateway config differed. What made the difference, and what would you put in front of the first one if the outage lasted ten minutes?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The difference is how the far end was unreachable. A closed port refuses immediately; a name that no longer resolves burns the resolver's timeout first. That cost belongs to whatever is between you and the processor, and `failureMode` has no opinion about it.

Over ten minutes, every routed request pays the full deadline while Jev is down, so a 1.5 second deadline adds 1.5 seconds to every request for ten minutes.

A breaker that opens after a few consecutive failures and serves the fallback directly turns that back into the near-free refusal we saw first. This rig hasn't got one, which is worth knowing before you copy it.

</details>

Put the stand-in and the environment back before the next section:

```bash
pkill -f jev_router.standin || true
sed -i '/JEV_BASE_URL/d;/JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS/d' router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
```

## Caching the decision, then measuring what the cache did

_~13 min · Hands-on_

You already saw the cache work, when a repeated request came back as `src=exact`.

That level keys on the normalised message plus everything else reaching Jev's state, so a hit answers the question the miss asked. Its hit rate is bounded by how much your traffic repeats.

The rig ships a second level, off by default, keyed on features instead: what the message asks for, how long it is, whether it carries code, how many tools came with it, and how deep the conversation runs.

Two requests that look alike share a key. Let's switch it on:

```bash
echo 'ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET=1' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
```

```console
$ echo 'ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET=1' >> router.env
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
 Container jev-router Recreate
 Container jev-router Recreated
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
 Container jev-router Waiting
 Container jev-router Healthy
$ docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
15:04:40 INFO    jev_router.server ext_proc listening on 0.0.0.0:9090 | jev=jev-latest | deadline=1.5s | cache exact=True bucket=True ttl=900s | policy=6ecdbc563f806f13
```

Two curls say nothing about a cache, so the rig carries a made-up week of coding-assistant traffic: twenty-two kinds of work, three ways of asking for each, and nothing on the surface of a message tracking which kind it is.

First we ask Jev about every distinct message once, which gives us something to grade the cache against:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.measure oracle
```

```console
asked Jev about 66 distinct messages
wrote oracle.json under policy 6ecdbc563f806f13
```

With no key there is nothing to ask, so the rig ships the file that command writes: copy `router/jev_router/fixtures/oracle.json` to `router/oracle.json` and the replay below grades against that.

Now replay a head-heavy stream of two hundred requests past both cache shapes, offline, and count the hits:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.measure replay --stream zipf
```

```console
corpus: deliberative 90, mechanical 110

stream zipf: 200 requests over 45 distinct messages

cache           keys    hit%  jev calls
exact             45   77.5%         45
exact+bucket      12   94.0%         12
```

Twelve keys covering two hundred requests, and the feature bucket took a good hit rate and made it a great one. This is where the change gets committed, so let's ask the other question first:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.measure replay --stream zipf --grade
```

```console
corpus: deliberative 90, mechanical 110

stream zipf: 200 requests over 45 distinct messages
graded against one fresh answer per distinct message

cache           keys    hit%  jev calls  agree on hits
exact             45   77.5%         45         100.0%
exact+bucket      12   94.0%         12          54.8%

5 buckets held requests that route two different ways:
  read|xs|prose|none|first     {'qwen-large': 27, 'qwen-small': 53}
  other|xs|prose|none|first    {'qwen-large': 13, 'qwen-small': 23}
  reason|s|prose|none|first    {'qwen-large': 17, 'qwen-small': 3}
  write|xs|prose|none|first    {'qwen-small': 7, 'qwen-large': 1}
  edit|s|prose|none|first      {'qwen-large': 1, 'qwen-small': 5}
whichever request lands first owns the bucket until the entry expires
```

On a two-option choice, agreeing on a little over half of the hits is no better than choosing at random.

Look at the last block. The buckets that hit most are the ones holding requests that route both ways, and whichever request arrives first owns the key until the entry expires.

The hits the bucket level scored came from the traffic repeating, and not from the key generalising across requests.

The exact level agrees on everything it serves by construction. It replays an answer to a state it was asked about, so it goes stale only when the underlying answer moves, which is what the fingerprint and the TTL are for.

So take it out:

```bash
sed -i '/ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET/d' router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
```

```console
$ sed -i '/ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET/d' router.env
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
 Container jev-router Recreate
 Container jev-router Recreated
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
 Container jev-router Waiting
 Container jev-router Healthy
$ docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
15:04:46 INFO    jev_router.server ext_proc listening on 0.0.0.0:9090 | jev=jev-latest | deadline=1.5s | cache exact=True bucket=False ttl=900s | policy=6ecdbc563f806f13
```

`bucket=False`, and the router is back to serving only answers it holds for the question it was asked.

<details>
<summary>Look closer: what happens when the traffic stops repeating</summary>

Replay the same corpus with every message sent exactly once:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.measure replay --stream unique --grade
```

```console
corpus: deliberative 36, mechanical 30

stream unique: 66 requests over 66 distinct messages
graded against one fresh answer per distinct message

cache           keys    hit%  jev calls  agree on hits
exact             66    0.0%         66              -
exact+bucket      13   80.3%         13          71.7%

5 buckets held requests that route two different ways:
  other|xs|prose|none|first    {'qwen-small': 11, 'qwen-large': 4}
  read|xs|prose|none|first     {'qwen-small': 5, 'qwen-large': 5}
  write|xs|prose|none|first    {'qwen-small': 3, 'qwen-large': 3}
  edit|s|prose|none|first      {'qwen-small': 2, 'qwen-large': 2}
  reason|s|prose|none|first    {'qwen-small': 1, 'qwen-large': 1}
whichever request lands first owns the bucket until the entry expires
```

The exact key hits nothing at all, which is the honest ceiling for a key that only serves repeats.

The bucket key carries on hitting most of the traffic on thirteen keys, and carries on being wrong about a large slice of it. Run both of these against a week of your own gateway's access log before you believe either number here.

</details>

Question: the agreement column is the reason the bucket level came out. Which of those two replay commands could you run against your own traffic tomorrow, and what would you need before the other one meant anything?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The hit-rate command runs against any log of request bodies, because counting keys needs no judgment at all. That's exactly why it's the tempting one, and on its own it recommends the worse key every time.

Grading needs an oracle, which means one fresh call per distinct message, paid once. That's the price of knowing whether your key carries the signal you assumed it did, and it's why a cache key deserves a measurement rather than a code review.

A key can be cheap to compute and easy to describe and still carry no routing signal at all.

</details>

## Teaching it a rule the criteria never carried

_~12 min · Hands-on_

Everything so far has graded the cache against Jev. Nothing has asked whether Jev agrees with anybody, and a cache can be perfect about an answer nobody wanted.

The corpus we've been replaying carries a label on every family, written by hand before any Jev call, so let's ask:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align grade --corpus corpus --oracle oracle.json
```

```console
policy 6ecdbc563f806f13, 66 messages graded by hand

kind            agrees   of      rate
deliberative        36   36   100.0%
mechanical          30   30   100.0%
overall             66   66   100.0%

every request went where the label says it should
```

Sixty-six out of sixty-six. That's what a policy looks like when the only judgement in it is the one already written down: the criteria were written for this traffic, and they separate it.

Now the traffic that started an argument. The rig carries twelve more families, every one of them touching money:

```python
HOUSE_RULE = (
    "Anything touching money goes to the larger model, however mechanical it looks."
)
```

A team that has had one bad refund migration decides that, and nothing in `policy.json` says it, because the criteria are about the reasoning a request needs rather than what it costs to get wrong.

Ask Jev about that traffic, and about sixteen ordinary requests from the corpus above so both sides of the line are in the same table, then grade the lot against the house rule:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align oracle --corpus mixed --out mixed-oracle.json
```

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align grade --corpus mixed --oracle mixed-oracle.json
```

```console
policy 6ecdbc563f806f13, 40 messages graded by hand

kind                            agrees   of      rate
money, reads as deliberative        12   12   100.0%
money, reads as mechanical           1   12     8.3%
ordinary deliberative                8    8   100.0%
ordinary mechanical                  8    8   100.0%
overall                             29   40    72.5%

11 disagreements, the first 6:
  rename-charge-field  label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.99)
    Rename `chargeAmount` to `amount_cents` across billing/ and update the callers.
  rename-charge-field  label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.97)
    In billing/, `chargeAmount` should be `amount_cents` everywhere it appears.
  price-list-format    label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.87)
    Convert this price list from JSON to YAML, keeping the key order.
  price-list-format    label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.97)
    Turn the attached tariff JSON into equivalent YAML.
  refund-type-hints    label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.78)
    Add type hints to every function in billing/refunds.py, including return types.
  refund-type-hints    label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.51)
    billing/refunds.py has no annotations. Add them.
```

Every ordinary request lands where its label says, and so does money work that obviously needs thinking. One in twelve on money work that reads as mechanical, and look at the confidence column: 0.99 that renaming a charge field is mechanical work.

Jev is reading the criteria correctly and answering the question it was asked. The criteria have simply never been told what a mistake costs here.

So this is not a model to correct. It's a policy this rig has never been told, and the fix is to write the rule into the criteria.

You could do that by hand, and for one rule you probably should. The interesting version is having something write it from examples of your judgement, which is what [jev-align](https://github.com/sutro-sh/jev-align) does: it shows you the requests Jev is least sure about, takes your label for each, and runs [GEPA](https://gepa-ai.github.io/gepa/) over your accumulated labels to propose new criteria.

GEPA is a reflective search: it reads what went wrong and writes the next candidate from that diagnosis. If you want to watch that loop run on something you can inspect line by line, the [GEPA lab](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=gepa-prompt-evolution&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-model-routing_readme) does exactly that.

Rewriting the criteria is one lever. The other leaves the wording alone and moves where Jev's probabilities get cut into a decision. If that's the one you're curious about, our [Compiling prompts with DSPy](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=dspy-programs&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-model-routing_readme) lab runs DSPy's ReAnchor optimiser over a Jev program and fits those cut-offs from labelled examples.

The pool it labels is forty requests, not the twenty-four above: the money-touching ones plus sixteen ordinary requests, half mechanical and half not. A pool where every answer is `qwen-large` teaches an optimiser to answer `qwen-large`, which is right about these twenty-four and wrong about the sixty-six the last section graded. A boundary needs both sides of it.

Install it, write out the traffic, and generate the command that starts from the policy this router is running:

```bash
uv tool install jev-align==0.1.4
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align export --corpus mixed --out pool.csv
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align seed --data pool.csv --batch-size 12
```

```console
wrote jeva-run.sh, which runs:

jeva optimize \
  pool.csv \
  --column message \
  --question 'Which model should answer `request.newest_message`? Judge only the newest message; `request.prior_turns` is context for what it refers to, never the thing being routed.' \
  --class 'qwen-small=The newest user message asks for a mechanical transformation that a competent engineer would finish without stopping to think: renaming or reformatting code, converting between two named formats, extracting values that are already written down in the message, translating prose, or answering a single factual question whose answer the message already contains. Length alone does not qualify a request for this option; a long but mechanical request still belongs here.' \
  --class 'qwen-large=The newest user message cannot be answered until something is worked out first: weighing a trade-off between two approaches, designing something that does not exist yet, diagnosing a fault from evidence that does not name the cause, reasoning about consequences the message does not state, or producing code whose correctness depends on a rule that has to be derived. Shortness does not disqualify a request from this option; a one-line question can still need deliberation.' \
  --jev-model 'jev-latest' \
  --batch-size 12 \
  --concurrency 6 \
  --max-metric-calls 120 \
  --reflection-model 'openrouter/anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5'

run it with `sh jeva-run.sh`; it asks you for every label.
```

The criteria in that command are the ones `policy.json` holds, read out of the file rather than typed again, so the search starts from the policy this router is running and every proposal it makes is a move away from that.

GEPA needs a model to write its proposals with. On a Zenable sandbox the hosted key covers that too, and the seed names the sandbox's model through OpenRouter. Anywhere else it's a second credential: `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `GEMINI_API_KEY` in `~/.env`, or `--reflection-model` naming any LiteLLM provider. `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is still what answers the questions.

The seed ran inside `router/`, so the script and `pool.csv` sit there, and that's where the run it starts will be saved. Start it from that directory:

```bash
(cd router && sh jeva-run.sh)
```

`jeva` takes over the terminal. It shows one request at a time with how uncertain Jev is about it, you pick a label with the arrow keys, and it asks for a rationale you can skip. Twelve of those, then GEPA reads your labels and proposes new criteria.

You accept or reject what it proposes, and a higher score on your own labels is not on its own a reason to accept: those labels are what the score is measured against.

Read the proposal before you take it. A proposal identical to the criteria you started with means the search found nothing to change, which is a real answer rather than a failure. It usually means you and the criteria already agree.

After you accept, `jeva` starts a second round of labels against the new criteria. You can stop there with Ctrl+C: it saves the run, and the criteria you accepted are already in it.

Once you have accepted one, install it:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align adopt .jev-align/runs/<run-id>
```

Without a key there is no run to adopt, so the rig ships the criteria this loop produced:

```bash
cp router/jev_router/fixtures/policy-aligned.json router/jev_router/policy.json
```

> [!NOTE]
> Those shipped criteria came from this same search, with the labels written by a model applying the house rule rather than by a person. Yours will differ, and they should: the point of the exercise is that your judgement is what the criteria end up describing.

Either way, `policy.json` now holds different text, so the question the router asks is a different question, and the fingerprint that names it has moved.

Every cache entry, every recorded decision and the oracle you built are filed under the old one, and none of them answer the new question. That is what the fingerprint is for: the router asks Jev afresh rather than replaying an answer to a question nobody asked.

So ask again, under the new criteria, and watch the first line of the output for the fingerprint they were asked under:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align oracle --corpus mixed --out mixed-aligned.json
```

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align grade --corpus mixed --oracle mixed-aligned.json
```

```console
policy 0e5de277d72abdf3, 40 messages graded by hand

kind                            agrees   of      rate
money, reads as deliberative        12   12   100.0%
money, reads as mechanical          12   12   100.0%
ordinary deliberative                8    8   100.0%
ordinary mechanical                  7    8    87.5%
overall                             39   40    97.5%

1 disagreements, the first 1:
  add-type-hints       label qwen-small  jev qwen-large (0.99)
    Add type hints to every function in billing/refunds.py, including the return types, and use the buil
```

72.5% to 97.5%, and the row that moved is the one the rule was about: money work that reads as mechanical went from one in twelve to twelve out of twelve. Ordinary deliberative work did not move, because nothing asked it to.

Now the interesting row. `ordinary mechanical` slipped from eight out of eight to seven, and the request it lost is worth reading:

```
add-type-hints  label qwen-small  jev qwen-large (0.99)
  Add type hints to every function in billing/refunds.py, including the return types
```

That request is in the ordinary half of the pool, labelled `qwen-small` because adding annotations is mechanical. It also names `billing/refunds.py`.

The criteria are applying the house rule correctly and the label is wrong. Whoever labelled that pool called it ordinary mechanical work because of what it does, and never noticed which file it does it to.

That is what a rule applied consistently does to a set of labels: it finds the ones you gave without thinking. The fix here is to the label, not to the criteria, and a real traffic sample would surface a dozen of these on the first pass.

Question: the criteria now route money work to the larger model, and every ordinary request still goes where it went before. What would tell you that this rewrite had gone too far, and which column here would show it?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The `ordinary mechanical` row. A criterion that reaches the money rule by widening what counts as serious work would drag renaming a variable and converting a JSON block along with it, and those are the requests the cheap model exists for.

Watch `ordinary deliberative` too. A rewrite can also go too far the other way, by sorting on money first and treating everything else as mechanical, and then the requests that needed the larger model lose it. Your own run can move either row, because your labels are what the search was measured against.

That row is in the table for exactly this reason. A pool of nothing but money requests would have scored a criterion reading "always use the larger model" at 100%, and the first ordinary request in production would have paid for it.

</details>

## Cleanup

_~2 min · Hands-on_

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
pkill -f jev_router.standin || true
docker compose down
rm -f router.env config.yaml mechanical.json deliberative.json standin.log
rm -f router/oracle.json router/mixed-oracle.json router/mixed-aligned.json router/pool.csv router/jeva-run.sh
rm -rf router/.jev-align
git checkout router/jev_router/policy.json
```

Then put Ollama back on loopback:

```bash
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/listen.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ollama
```

The two models stay on disk. `ollama rm qwen3:0.6b` takes the smaller one back if you want the space. If you're on a workshop VM, terminating the instance is enough. Thanks for building with us!
